title: The True Cost of an H-1B Visa in 2026: Courts, Fees, and a Shifting Lottery
excerpt: Between a contested $100,000 surcharge, a new wage-weighted lottery, and rising subcontracting costs, sponsoring an H-1B worker has never been more expensive or uncertain for employers and Indian professionals.
body:
• A federal court struck down the $100,000 H-1B fee in June 2026, but a stay reinstated it while the government appeals — leaving employers in legal limbo
  • A new wage-weighted lottery system, effective February 2026, favours higher-paid roles and could cut selection chances for entry-level workers by 48%
  • India's top IT firms have already slashed H-1B filings by 56% over the past decade, accelerating the shift to offshore delivery and local hiring
  • Indians hold roughly 71% of all H-1B approvals, making every cost increase and policy shift a direct hit on the diaspora

The H-1B visa has never been cheap or easy to get. In 2026, it has become a programme mired in litigation, escalating costs, and regulatory overhauls that have left employers, immigration lawyers, and Indian tech professionals scrambling to keep up.

The headline number — a $100,000 surcharge on new H-1B petitions — has dominated coverage since President Trump signed Proclamation 10973 in September 2025. But that fee is only one layer of a system where the ground is shifting under every participant's feet.

The $100,000 Fee: Struck Down, Then Revived

On June 8, 2026, U.S. District Judge Leo Sorokin in Massachusetts ruled the $100,000 fee unlawful, calling it a revenue-generating tax that exceeded presidential authority. The ruling in California et al. v. Trump vacated the fee entirely — a victory for the 20 states that had argued it was devastating staffing at universities, hospitals, and research institutions.

The relief lasted four days. On June 12, Judge Sorokin issued an administrative stay of his own ruling while the Trump administration appealed to the First Circuit. The fee remains in effect, and employers must continue paying it for new H-1B petitions involving consular processing. The appeal's outcome will determine whether the fee survives or whether employers can seek refunds for the hundreds of millions already collected.

"This $100,000 fee will advantage big tech companies that can afford it while shutting out smaller companies and startups, essentially concentrating talent and power among the tech giants."

— Hemant Mohapatra, Partner, Lightspeed India

A New Lottery That Favours Higher Salaries

Separately, a new DHS rule that took effect in February 2026 replaced the random H-1B lottery with a wage-weighted selection process. Registrations for roles paying Level 4 wages now have a 107% higher chance of being selected compared with the old system. Level 1 wage registrations — the category most common among entry-level engineers from India — face a 48% decrease in selection probability.

The rule means employers must lock in occupation codes, wage levels, and worksite geography before registration, turning what was once a compliance formality into a strategic workforce decision. For Indian IT services firms that frequently deployed junior and mid-level engineers on H-1B visas, the new system all but forces a model change.

Indian IT Firms Already Adapting

Data from the National Foundation for American Policy shows that India's six largest IT services companies — TCS, Infosys, HCL Technologies, Wipro, Tech Mahindra, and LTIMindtree — have collectively reduced H-1B visa filings by 56% over the past decade. TCS sponsored 5,505 H-1B visas in 2025, down from 10,525 in 2021.

The shift has accelerated a move toward offshore delivery and local hiring. Three of India's top five IT firms reported more than 20% year-over-year increases in subcontracting costs in the December 2025 quarter, according to The Hindu BusinessLine. TCS saw subcontractor spending rise 26.6% to ₹3,560 crore.

"Subcontracting has now become an operational necessity with higher visa fees and longer processing times," said Phil Fersht, CEO of HFS Research. "Firms are increasingly relying on locally hired subcontractors in client geographies."

What It Means for the Diaspora

For the roughly 600,000 Indian-born H-1B holders currently in the United States, the cumulative effect of these changes extends beyond cost. The wage-weighted lottery makes it harder for younger professionals to enter the system. The $100,000 fee, if it survives appeal, prices out startups and mid-sized employers from sponsoring new workers. And the ongoing shift toward Global Capability Centres in India means fewer slots overall.

JPMorgan economists have estimated the $100,000 fee alone could reduce work authorisations by up to 5,500 per month. Amitabh Kant, India's former NITI Aayog CEO, put it bluntly on X: "Donald Trump's 100,000 H-1B fee will choke U.S. innovation, and turbocharge India's."

The legal battle continues. But for Indian professionals navigating the system today, the message is clear: the H-1B is neither cheap, nor convenient, nor certain.
image_caption: The H-1B visa programme faces its most uncertain period in decades as legal battles and policy changes pile up
nri_angle: Indian professionals account for 71% of all H-1B approvals, making every cost increase and policy shift a direct concern for hundreds of thousands of families across the U.S.
author: Diaspora Desk
